danish.title: Første bog (1805) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Stilheden sænkede sig. Grevinden betragtede sine gæster med et venligt smil, men uden at skjule, at hun ikke ville have noget imod, hvis de nu rejste sig og tog deres afsked. Gæstens datter glattede allerede sin kjole med et spørgende blik til sin mor, da man pludselig fra det tilstødende værelse hørte lyden af drenge og piger, der løb hen mod døren, en stol der væltede, og en pige på tretten, der skjulte noget i folderne af sin korte muslinkjole, stormede ind og standsede brat midt i stuen. Det var tydeligt, at hun ikke havde haft til hensigt at løbe så langt. Bag hende i døråbningen dukkede en student med rød uniformskrave op, en gardesofficer, en pige på femten og en buttet, rosenkindede dreng i kort jakke.
Greven sprang op, vuggede fra side til side, bredte armene ud og lagde dem om den lille pige, der var løbet ind.
»Nå, der har vi hende!« udbrød han leende. »Min skat, som har navnedag. Min kære lille skat!«
»Ma chère, der er tid og sted for alting,« sagde grevinden med påtaget strenghed. »Du forkæler hende, Ilja,« tilføjede hun og vendte sig mod sin mand.
»Goddag, min kære! Tillykke med navnedagen,« sagde gæsten. »Sikke et henrivende barn,« tilføjede hun henvendt til moderen.

Denne sortøjede, bredmundede pige — ikke køn, men fuld af liv — med bare barneskuldre, der efter løbet hævede sig og rystede hendes korset, med sorte krøller kastet bagover, tynde bare arme, små ben i kniplingsbesatte underbukser og fødder i lave tøfler — var netop på den charmerende alder, hvor en pige ikke længere er et barn, men endnu heller ikke en ung kvinde. Hun slap fri af sin fars arme og løb hen for at skjule sit rødmende ansigt i sin mors mantilles blonder — uden at ænse den strenge bemærkning det mindste — og begyndte at le. Hun lo, og i afbrudte sætninger forsøgte hun at forklare noget om en dukke, som hun trak frem af kjolens folder.

»Kan du se?... Min dukke... Mimi... Ser du...« var alt, Natasja (Natasha) fik stammende sagt, for hende virkede alting komisk. Hun lænede sig op ad sin mor og brast ud i en så højlydt, klingende latter, at selv den fornemme gæst ikke kunne lade være med at stemme i.
»Så, gå nu væk og tag dit monstrum med dig,« sagde moderen og skubbede datteren fra sig med påtaget strenghed, før hun vendte sig mod gæsten og tilføjede: »Hun er min yngste pige.«
Natasja løftede et øjeblik ansigtet fra sin mors mantille, kiggede op på hende gennem lattermilde tårer og gemte sit ansigt igen.
Gæsten, som var nødt til at overvære denne familiescene, syntes det var passende at tage del i den.
»Sig mig, min kære,« sagde hun til Natasja, »er Mimi i familie med dig? En datter, formoder jeg?«
Natasja brød sig ikke om gæstens nedladende tone over for barnlige ting. Hun svarede ikke, men så alvorligt på hende.

I mellemtiden havde den yngre generation — Boris (Anna Mikhajlovnas søn), gardesofficeren; Nikolaj (Nikolai), grevens ældste søn og universitetsstuderende; Sonja (Sonia), grevens femtenårige niece; og lille Petja, hans yngste dreng — alle slået sig ned i dagligstuen og forsøgte åbenbart at holde den begejstring og munterhed, der lyste ud af alle deres ansigter, inden for sømmelighedens grænser. Det var tydeligt, at samtalen i baglokalerne, hvorfra de var stormet så voldsomt, havde været langt morsommere end dagligstuens snak om skandaler, vejr og grevinde Apraksina. Nu og da skævede de til hinanden og kunne næppe undertrykke deres latter.

De to unge mænd, studenten og officeren, barndomsvenner af samme alder, var begge flotte fyre, men ikke ens. Boris var høj og lyshåret med et roligt, smukt ansigt og regelmæssige, fine træk. Nikolaj var kort med krøllet hår og et åbent udtryk. Mørkt skæg var allerede ved at vise sig på hans overlæbe, og hele hans ansigt udtrykte heftighed og begejstring. Nikolaj rødmede, da han trådte ind i dagligstuen. Han forsøgte tydeligvis at finde noget at sige, men kunne ikke. Boris derimod fandt straks sit fodfæste og fortalte stille og humoristisk, hvordan han havde kendt dukken Mimi, da hun endnu var en ganske ung dame, før hendes næse var gået i stykker; hvordan hun var ældet i de fem år, han havde kendt hende, og hvordan hendes hoved var revnet tværs over kraniet. Da han sagde dette, kastede han et blik på Natasja. Hun vendte sig bort fra ham og kiggede på sin lillebror, der kneb øjnene sammen og rystede af undertrykt latter, og da hun ikke længere kunne holde sig, sprang hun op og styrtede ud af stuen, så hurtigt hendes lette små fødder kunne bære hende. Boris lo ikke.
»Du ville gerne ud, ikke, Mamma? Skal jeg sige, de skal gøre vognen klar?« spurgte han sin mor med et smil.
»Ja, ja, gå hen og sig til dem, de skal gøre den klar,« svarede hun og gengældte hans smil.
Boris forlod stille stuen og gik ud for at lede efter Natasja. Den buttede dreng løb vredt efter dem, som om han var irriteret over, at deres plan var blevet forstyrret.

english.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Silence fell over the room. The countess looked at her guests with a pleasant smile, though she made no effort to hide the fact that she wouldn't be upset if they got up and left. The visitor's daughter was already smoothing down her dress and glancing at her mother when suddenly, from the next room, came the sound of boys and girls running toward the door, a chair toppling over, and a thirteen-year-old girl burst in, clutching something hidden in the folds of her short muslin dress, and stopped dead in the middle of the room. She had clearly not meant to run this far. Behind her in the doorway appeared a university student with a crimson collar, a Guards officer, a fifteen-year-old girl, and a plump, rosy-faced boy in a short jacket.
The count leapt to his feet and, swaying side to side, threw his arms wide open around the little girl who had come running in.
"There she is!" he cried, laughing. "My darling, the birthday girl! My sweetheart!"
"My dear, there is a time and place for everything," the countess said with pretended sternness. "You spoil her, Ilya," she added, turning to her husband.
"How do you do, my dear? Happy name day to you," said the visitor. "What a delightful child," she added, turning to the mother.

This black-eyed, wide-mouthed girl — not pretty, but bursting with life — with her childish bare shoulders still heaving from running, her bodice shaking, black curls tossed back, thin bare arms, little legs in lace-trimmed drawers, and feet in low slippers — was at that enchanting age when a girl is no longer a child but not yet a young woman. Breaking free from her father, she ran to bury her flushed face in the lace of her mother's shawl, completely ignoring the stern remark, and began to laugh. Through broken sentences she tried to explain something about a doll she pulled from the folds of her dress.

"Look!... My doll... Mimi... Look..." was all Natasha could manage to say — everything struck her as hilarious. She leaned against her mother and burst into such a loud, ringing fit of laughter that even the prim visitor couldn't help joining in.
"Now then, off you go and take your little monster with you," said the mother, pushing her daughter away with mock severity, and turning to the visitor she added: "She's my youngest."
Natasha raised her face from her mother's shawl for a moment, glanced up through tears of laughter, and buried her face again.
The visitor, forced to witness this family scene, felt obliged to take some part in it.
"Tell me, my dear," she said to Natasha, "is Mimi a relation of yours? A daughter, I suppose?"
Natasha didn't like the visitor's condescending tone toward childish things. She made no reply and just looked at her seriously.

Meanwhile the younger generation — Boris, the officer, Anna Mikhaylovna's son; Nicholas, the university student, the count's eldest son; Sonya, the count's fifteen-year-old niece; and little Petya, his youngest boy — had all settled into the drawing room and were clearly trying to contain the excitement and laughter shining in all their faces within the bounds of good manners. Obviously the conversation in the back rooms, from which they had burst out so eagerly, had been far more entertaining than the drawing room talk of society scandals, weather, and Countess Apraksina. Now and then they glanced at each other, barely able to hold back their laughter.

The two young men, the student and the officer, childhood friends, were the same age and both good-looking, though quite different. Boris was tall and fair, with a calm, handsome face and regular, refined features. Nicholas was shorter, with curly hair and an open expression. Dark hairs were already showing above his lip, and his whole face radiated energy and enthusiasm. Nicholas blushed when he entered the drawing room. He obviously tried to think of something to say but couldn't. Boris, on the other hand, found his footing immediately and began telling — calmly and with humor — how he had known the doll Mimi when she was still quite a young lady, before her nose was broken, how she had aged in the five years he'd known her, and how her head had cracked right across the skull. As he spoke he glanced at Natasha. She turned away from him and looked at her younger brother, who was screwing up his eyes and shaking with suppressed laughter, and, unable to hold herself back any longer, she leapt up and dashed from the room as fast as her nimble little feet could carry her. Boris did not laugh.
"You were about to go out, weren't you, Mama? Shall I have the carriage brought round?" he asked his mother with a smile.
"Yes, yes, go and tell them to get it ready," she replied, returning his smile.
Boris quietly left the room and went to find Natasha. The plump boy ran after them, annoyed that their plans had been disrupted.
